column1: # SAFE_CMDS coverage matrix: every command in the TEXT/SEARCH/FORMAT/
# INSPECT/CHECKSUM/FS/PROC/SYS/DEV groups, tested bare (no path) and
# with a path argument. Purpose: lock in which commands carry a
# file-path deny carve-out (cat/head/tail/grep/rg, plus sed -n) versus
# which stay allowed even with a path arg. A regression in any
# file-deny rule, or accidental removal of a command from SAFE_CMDS,
# --- TEXT_CMDS: cat/head/tail have a file-path deny; the rest do not ---
# (awk is intentionally absent -- denied entirely, covered above.)
# sed: bare and plain-path allowed; only `sed -n <range> <file>` denies.
# --- SEARCH_CMDS: grep/rg have a file-path deny; jq does not ---
# The SAFE_CMDS allow rule is `^(${SAFE_CMDS})\b` -- NO ${TOOL_PATH} --
# so an absolute-path invocation does NOT match the allow. Result:
#   - cat/head/tail: passthrough bare (cat-deny needs a trailing '/'),
#     deny with a path arg (cat-deny carries ${TOOL_PATH}).
#   - grep/rg: deny either way -- the dedicated absolute-path grep deny
#   - sed: passthrough bare and with a plain path; `sed -n <range>
#   - every other safe command: passthrough -- no allow match, no deny.
# These passthrough rows are a deliberate monitored gap: absolute-path
# benign tools are not auto-allowed. If that policy ever changes (e.g.
# ${TOOL_PATH} added to the SAFE_CMDS allow), these rows flip and flag it.
# --- absolute-path: cat/head/tail (deny only with a path arg) ---
# --- absolute-path: all other safe commands -> passthrough ---
